title: Zoning out while someone is talking
source_document: ADDitude: Are You Listening? (Novotni; published 2007, updated May 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Source notes the 2025 update looks like the 2007 content.
text:
Recognize it when: your mind drifts while someone talks and you miss half of it.
Technique: use small active-listening moves that keep your attention busy.
How: 1. Picture the story as they tell it, and imagine being asked about it later.
2. Nod or say a short 'mm-hm' so you stay engaged.
3. Keep your reply to one point they made, not every tangent.
4. Write 2 or 3 keywords if it is a meeting.
5. If you lose the thread, say: Can you repeat that last part?
Why it helps: Active moves give your attention a job. Asking to repeat is normal and shows you care.
Try saying: Sorry, I drifted for a second. Can you say that last part again?
If it does not work: ask a trusted person for a private signal when you drift, or record the conversation if it is allowed.

title: A notepad for thoughts that pull you away
source_document: ADDitude: Manage Your Distractions (Silver); Understood: How to focus with ADHD (updated Apr 2026); NHS Berkshire inattention guide
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: your own thoughts keep interrupting what you are doing, and you worry you will forget them.
Technique: write the stray thought on a notepad or phone note and go back to the task.
How: 1. Keep a note open or a pad on your desk.
2. When a thought pulls you, write 3 to 5 words.
3. Return to the task at once.
4. Review the list at a set time (end of the work block).
5. Reward yourself for letting each thought go.
Why it helps: The fear of forgetting is what makes a thought hard to drop. A written note takes that fear away.
Try saying: It is saved. I can come back to it at 3.
If it does not work: if writing breaks your focus, use a single word.

title: Phone and noise keep pulling you away
source_document: Cleveland Clinic: How to Focus with ADHD (Feb 2025); Understood: How to focus with ADHD (Apr 2026); CHADD attention strategies infographic
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Several mechanisms stated in these pages (e.g. dopamine) are simplified.
text:
Recognize it when: every notification or noise pulls you away from what you were doing.
Technique: remove the pull before you start, rather than relying on willpower.
How: 1. Turn off notifications or put your phone in another room.
2. Use a blocker app for sites you slide into.
3. Use noise-cancelling earphones or low steady background sound.
4. Put the block on your calendar and tell people nearby.
5. Do the hardest task in your best hours.
Why it helps: Willpower is unreliable in ADHD, but removing the trigger works without it.
Try saying: I will remove the pull, not fight it.
If it does not work: if you need the phone, set two check times instead of constant access.

title: Does background or white noise help focus? (small evidence)
source_document: CHADD ADHD Weekly: White Noise for Staying On Task (Mar 2020); Cleveland Clinic: How to Focus with ADHD
source_citation: CHADD cites small studies, mostly in children; benefits did not persist after noise stopped and evidence is inconclusive.
text:
Recognize it when: it is too quiet to focus, or noise bothers you.
Technique: try steady low sound (fan, rain, brown or pink noise, instrumental music) and keep it only if it helps.
How: 1. Try one type for 20 minutes.
2. If you get more done, keep it. If it distracts, stop.
3. Avoid lyrics or speech (babble made tasks harder in one study).
4. Do not expect it to fix impulsivity.
Why it helps: Some people with ADHD work better with steady sound, but studies are small and mostly in children, so test it for yourself.
Try saying: I will test it for 20 minutes and see.
If it does not work: if noise irritates you, use earplugs or work in a quiet room.

title: Plan breaks before your focus fades
source_document: Understood: How to focus with ADHD; Cleveland Clinic: How to Focus with ADHD; ADDA: Tips for Studying with ADHD
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Pomodoro has no ADHD trial in these sources; adjust the interval to yourself.
text:
Recognize it when: you work until you are fried, or you keep losing focus after a short time.
Technique: use a visible timer and short breaks planned in advance.
How: 1. Set a timer for 20 to 25 minutes (adjust to your attention).
2. Work on one thing only.
3. When it rings, take a 5-minute break: walk, stretch, water. Avoid scrolling.
4. After four rounds take a longer break.
5. If you are in flow, snooze the alarm.
Why it helps: Planned breaks prevent burnout and the timer gives time an outside shape.
Try saying: One round. Then a break.
If it does not work: shorten the work block to 10 minutes.

title: Hyperfocus on the wrong thing: how to stop
source_document: Understood: Understanding ADHD and hyperfocus (Apr 2026); ADDitude: Hyperfocus (updated Aug 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Hyperfocus is not an official ADHD symptom.
text:
Recognize it when: you lose hours to a game, video or hobby and miss what you needed to do.
Technique: set exit cues before you start and make the switch gradual.
How: 1. Decide a stop time before starting.
2. Set two alarms, one before the end.
3. Stop at a natural break (end of an episode or level).
4. Ask someone to tap you or message you.
5. Put a small buffer task between the fun task and the next (stretch, water).
6. Remove the trigger if needed (log out, unplug).
Why it helps: Time sense is weak in hyperfocus. Outside cues and a gradual switch make stopping realistic.
Try saying: Alarm set. I stop at the end of this episode.
If it does not work: ask a person to physically check in with you at the end time.

title: Time blindness: make time visible
source_document: Cleveland Clinic: Time blindness (2023); ADDitude: How ADHD Warps Time Perception (Tuckman); ADDA: ADHD Time Blindness (2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. ADDA cites background studies but none test the listed tips.
text:
Recognize it when: you always underestimate how long things take or are surprised by the time.
Technique: use outside time cues and buffers.
How: 1. Put analog clocks or timers in rooms you use.
2. Add about 10 extra minutes per 30 you estimate.
3. Set calendar alerts before the real deadline.
4. Put timed tasks on the calendar rather than an open list.
5. For 3 days log what you did in 30-minute slots, then review.
Why it helps: Logging shows real durations, and buffers protect you from your own underestimates.
Try saying: Real time is longer than my guess. I will add a buffer.
If it does not work: start with one clock and one alarm.

title: Zoning out in class or while studying
source_document: Bowdoin College Baldwin Center: Focusing in Class and During Study; Novotni (ADDitude)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Not ADHD-specific.
text:
Recognize it when: your mind drifts in lectures or while reading and you lose your place.
Technique: prepare before class, stay active during it, and give daydreaming its own time.
How: 1. Before class skim the topic and write 2 questions.
2. Sit near the front, phone silent.
3. Take handwritten notes or draw diagrams; ask a question.
4. After class write a 3-line summary.
5. If you drift, note where you stopped and move on. Schedule a daydream break later.
Why it helps: Preparation makes the material familiar, and active note-taking gives your attention a job.
Try saying: I drifted. I will mark where I lost it and catch up after class.
If it does not work: ask a friend to share notes for the missed part.

title: Quick anger: catch it in your body, then pause
source_document: ADDitude: Crashing Out? How to Calm Down When You're Angry (Saline, Sep 2025); Cleveland Clinic: ADHD and emotional dysregulation (Mar 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you snap quickly and regret it.
Technique: learn your early body signals and use a pause with one calming action.
How: 1. Notice early signs: tight stomach, hot face, fast breathing, louder voice.
2. Say: I need a moment.
3. Leave the room or pause the task.
4. Use one soother: cold water on hands, a walk, breathe in 4 hold 4 out 6.
5. Come back once your body is calmer.
Why it helps: Anger starts in the body before thinking, so early signs give you the most room to act.
Try saying: I need a minute. I will come back.
If it does not work: practise on mild annoyance, so it works when you are really angry.

title: Turn anger into a clear request: Feeling, Issue, Behaviour
source_document: CHADD Attention: How to Be Angry Better (Malen, Apr 2019)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. The FIB sequence is a clinician's model, not tested.
text:
Recognize it when: you get angry and then argue instead of solving the problem.
Technique: after you pause, name the feeling, name the issue, and ask for a specific behaviour.
How: 1. Notice you are angry and pause.
2. Name the feeling without judging it.
3. Name the issue: what you want and what is blocking it.
4. Choose a behaviour that solves it.
5. Say: I feel __ about __. Could you please __?
Why it helps: Outbursts rarely fix the problem. A calm request does.
Try saying: I feel frustrated about the plan changing. Could you tell me earlier next time?
If it does not work: write the sentence first, then say it.

title: Repair after you snapped at someone
source_document: Understood: The ADHD shame spiral from making mistakes in relationships (Feb 2025); ADDitude: How to Hit Pause on ADHD Impulsivity (Barkley)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you said something harsh and want to fix it without a shame spiral.
Technique: a short repair: acknowledge, name the impact, apologise, ask what helps, then act differently.
How: 1. Wait until you are calm.
2. Acknowledge their feelings.
3. Name the impact: I know that hurt.
4. Apologise for how it landed. Share your intent only briefly.
5. Ask what would help.
6. Show change in action, not just words.
Why it helps: A calm, specific repair builds trust and keeps shame from taking over.
Try saying: I am sorry I snapped. I know it hurt. What would help?
If it does not work: if you are too upset, agree a 10 to 20 minute break and return.

title: Agree a time-out in advance
source_document: Understood: The ADHD shame spiral from making mistakes in relationships (Feb 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: arguments escalate quickly and you say things you do not mean.
Technique: agree on a pause when you are calm so it does not feel like avoidance.
How: 1. With a partner or friend, agree on a phrase (I need a break).
2. Agree the length (10 to 20 minutes) and that you will come back.
3. Use the phrase early.
4. Calm your body, then return and restart.
Why it helps: A pre-agreed break prevents the other person from feeling abandoned and gives you time to settle.
Try saying: I need a 15 minute break. I will come back.
If it does not work: write the plan down together.

title: Restlessness: movement bursts and quiet fidgets
source_document: Understood: Understanding hyperactivity; CHADD Attention: Fidgeting (Rotz, Feb 2025); CHADD: Don't Stop the Movement (2016)
source_citation: Small studies, mostly children; some citations in CHADD piece do not match; mechanisms speculative.
text:
Recognize it when: you cannot sit still or feel an inner buzz.
Technique: give your body a planned outlet.
How: 1. Take a 2-minute burst: jumping jacks, run in place, stretch.
2. Do active chores or a short walk.
3. Keep a quiet fidget (putty, ring, rubber band).
4. Doodle with rhythmic shading.
5. Avoid noisy fidgets that bother others.
Why it helps: A short burst of movement can satisfy the urge and make it easier to sit afterward.
Try saying: I will move for two minutes then sit.
If it does not work: if restlessness is constant, discuss it with a clinician.

title: Feeling bored or understimulated while working
source_document: ADDA: A Guide to Understimulated ADHD (Oct 2023); Understood: ADHD and the boredom spiral (Jul 2026)
source_citation: 'Understimulated ADHD' is a popular label, not a diagnosis; dopamine explanations are simplified; techniques not tested.
text:
Recognize it when: tasks feel dull, you scroll, snack or look for something stimulating.
Technique: add safe stimulation to the task and plan a break.
How: 1. Add low music, a body double or a fidget.
2. Change your place or rearrange your desk.
3. Use a timer and make a mini challenge.
4. Put the task down, do something enjoyable for 10 minutes, then return.
5. Notice if boredom is leading to scrolling or impulsive spending.
Why it helps: Making a dull task a bit more engaging lowers the pull to escape it.
Try saying: This is boring, not impossible. I will add some stimulation.
If it does not work: if nothing interests you even in things you love, see the numbness chunk.

title: Feeling flat or numb: when it is more than boredom
source_document: CHADD ADHD Weekly: When Depression Co-occurs with ADHD (Jul 2019); ADDitude: ADHD or Depression? (May 2022); Understood: ADHD and the boredom spiral (Jul 2026)
source_citation: Mixed clinician and personal sources. ADHD-related low mood usually lifts with engagement; depression is more pervasive. This is not a diagnosis.
text:
Recognize it when: you feel numb, flat, empty or disconnected.
Technique: check whether the flatness lifts with interesting things, and seek help if it does not.
How: 1. Ask: do things I normally love still feel good? If not, that is a warning sign.
2. Note how long it has lasted. About two weeks or more means talk to a clinician.
3. If it came after a medication change, tell your prescriber. Do not change medication alone.
4. Do one small thing: a walk, a message to a friend.
5. If you have thoughts of harming yourself or feel hopeless, contact a crisis line or emergency services now.
Why it helps: ADHD boredom lifts with engagement, while depression stays. Being honest about this protects you.
Try saying: I feel flat. I will check how long and tell someone.
If it does not work: if you think you are in danger, call your local emergency number or crisis line right away.

title: Name the emotion and track triggers
source_document: Cleveland Clinic: ADHD and emotional dysregulation (Mar 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. EFT tapping mentioned in source has no evidence given.
text:
Recognize it when: emotions feel big and you do not know why.
Technique: name the emotion precisely and keep a short trigger log.
How: 1. Name the exact emotion (frustrated, jealous, hurt).
2. Ask: what happened just before, what is underneath, where do I feel it?
3. Pause 5 to 10 minutes with box breathing or a body scan.
4. Log trigger, feeling, what helped.
5. Look for patterns weekly.
Why it helps: Naming and tracking turn a flood into information you can plan for.
Try saying: What is the exact feeling and what set it off?
If it does not work: if reactions are intense or hurt work and relationships, consider CBT or DBT.

title: After a mistake: Name, Place, Repair, Reconfigure
source_document: ADDitude: Your Regret Won't Change the Past (Saline, Jun 2022, updated May 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. EMDR, EFT and Ho'oponopono mentioned without evidence.
text:
Recognize it when: you made a mistake and replay it for hours.
Technique: four steps to move from regret to action.
How: 1. Name the specific regret. Separate 'I did a bad thing' from 'I am bad'.
2. Place it in context (stress, circumstances) while owning your part.
3. Repair: listen, decide what applies, choose a concrete way to make amends.
4. Reconfigure: choose a new response and ask what support you need.
Why it helps: Splitting act from identity reduces shame and points toward a fix.
Try saying: I did something I regret. It does not define me. What is my repair?
If it does not work: if shame is heavy and constant, talk to a therapist.

title: Self-compassion after you mess up
source_document: ADDitude: How to Practice Self-Compassion with ADHD (Saline, Sep 2021, updated May 2025); Understood: ADHD and Shame (Jan 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Kristin Neff's three-part model of self-compassion.
text:
Recognize it when: you call yourself stupid or a failure after a mistake.
Technique: use three parts: kindness, shared humanity, mindfulness.
How: 1. Notice the feeling without judging it (mindfulness).
2. Remind yourself that many people struggle with this (shared humanity).
3. Say what you would say to a 10-year-old who made the same mistake (kindness).
4. Give the inner critic a name or colour and answer back.
5. Then fix what can be fixed.
Why it helps: Kindness lowers shame so you can solve the problem, rather than hiding.
Try saying: Everyone struggles with this. What would I say to a friend?
If it does not work: keep a list of qualities you value somewhere you see it.

title: Restart after a shame spiral
source_document: Understood: The ADHD shame spiral from making mistakes in relationships (Feb 2025); Understood: ADHD and Shame (Jan 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Coach-level evidence.
text:
Recognize it when: one mistake has you thinking you will never get it right.
Technique: separate what happened from the story and set a 'do' goal.
How: 1. Write what happened in one neutral sentence.
2. Write the story you added ('I always ruin things').
3. Replace 'don't' goals with 'do' goals (I will check twice).
4. Take one small action today.
5. Tell one safe person.
Why it helps: Zero-mistake targets raise anxiety. A concrete 'do' goal moves you forward.
Try saying: One mistake is an event. Let me choose one small action.
If it does not work: if the same spiral keeps returning, therapy can help.

title: Scripts to ask your boss for help or feedback
source_document: Understood: Not sure how to ask your boss for help? Sentence starters (Touger, updated Mar 2023); ADD Resource Center: Advocate for Yourself at Work (Feb 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you avoid asking for help or feedback because you fear looking incompetent.
Technique: use a short script that links your request to the work.
How: 1. Pick a calm moment such as a one-on-one.
2. Say: I want to do my best work. Can we talk about __?
3. Or: I am struggling with __. I would like to try __. Are you OK with that?
4. Ask: What is one thing I could improve?
5. Write the answer down. If speaking is hard, send it by email.
Why it helps: Specific, goal-linked requests are easier to answer and show commitment.
Try saying: Could I get your advice on how to handle this?
If it does not work: rehearse the sentence once aloud.

title: Asking a professor or teacher for help
source_document: Understood: 6 phrases to use when asking your professor for support; UNC Learning Center: Emailing Professors
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you fear asking a teacher for help or extra time.
Technique: use office hours and a short email.
How: 1. Go early in the term and say what helps (extra time, a signal).
2. In office hours ask: Can you explain this a different way?
3. For email, use a specific subject line and 3 to 5 sentences.
4. Wait an hour before sending a heated email.
5. If needed, ask your disability office.
Why it helps: Office hours are less rushed than class, and a short clear email is easier to answer.
Try saying: Could we meet in your office hours to go through this?
If it does not work: start with one low-stakes question.

title: Can't start an assignment: the 10-minute rule
source_document: LSE student wellbeing: Studying at LSE, a guide for students with AD(H)D
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you avoid starting an essay or assignment.
Technique: commit to 10 minutes, then decide whether to stop.
How: 1. Set a 10-minute timer and open the document.
2. Predict one distraction and decide how to handle it.
3. When it rings, decide: continue or stop.
4. Set a mini-deadline for the next step (topic, research, first draft).
Why it helps: Starting is the hardest part, and the stop option makes it feel safe.
Try saying: Just ten minutes.
If it does not work: shrink to 2 minutes and write one sentence.

title: Study by testing yourself (backed by a study with ADHD students)
source_document: Minear et al., Frontiers in Psychology (2023): Is practice good enough? Retrieval benefits students with ADHD; ADDA: Tips for Studying with ADHD
source_citation: Minear et al. (2023), Frontiers in Psychology, PMC10397724: 36 college students with self-reported ADHD vs 36 controls, word pairs. Small sample, self-reported diagnosis.
text:
Recognize it when: you reread notes and still forget them.
Technique: close the book, recall, check, then revisit gaps.
How: 1. Read a section once and close it.
2. Write or say what you remember.
3. Check and mark gaps.
4. Add meaning (a picture or example) for the gaps.
5. Repeat on later days, spaced out.
Why it helps: Testing beat restudying for students with ADHD in this study, but they also needed deeper encoding at first.
Try saying: Close the notes and test myself.
If it does not work: use flashcards or past papers.

title: Pomodoro and body doubling for study (weak evidence)
source_document: ADDA: Tips for Studying with ADHD (Aug 2023); Fairfield University library guide (2026); Neurodiversity in Business report (Mar 2026)
source_citation: No ADHD trials found for Pomodoro or body doubling; a sponsored 117-adult before-and-after report had no control group.
text:
Recognize it when: you cannot study alone.
Technique: work alongside someone in short timed blocks.
How: 1. Say your goal at the start.
2. Work 25 minutes while the other person works in silence (in person or on camera).
3. Take 5 minutes break.
4. Reward yourself after the block.
Why it helps: Shared presence adds external structure and lowers the urge to wander. Evidence is plausible but weak.
Try saying: I will study next to a friend for 25 minutes.
If it does not work: use a study live-stream if no one is available.

title: Essay writing: draft first, polish later
source_document: UNC Writing Center: ADHD and Graduate Writing (Jun 2026); LSE ADHD study guide
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you edit every sentence as you write and never finish.
Technique: separate drafting and polishing into different sessions.
How: 1. Brainstorm as a list of questions to answer.
2. Talk or dictate the ideas.
3. Turn off the monitor or ignore edits and write for a set time.
4. Another day, polish.
5. Read it aloud and make a reverse outline to check logic.
Why it helps: Drafting and editing use different mental modes. Mixing them stalls writing.
Try saying: First draft is allowed to be rough.
If it does not work: ask a friend to check the main argument only.

title: Exam stress: breathe and practise timed papers
source_document: Fairfield University: Neurodiverse Study Hacks; LSE ADHD study guide
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you panic or freeze in an exam.
Technique: practise under timing and use a short breathing reset.
How: 1. Before exams do timed past papers.
2. In the exam, put your pencil down and breathe in for 3, hold 3, out 3, for a few rounds.
3. Start with the question you know best.
4. Arrange adjustments early.
Why it helps: Practising in exam conditions makes the real thing familiar, and breathing calms the panic.
Try saying: Pencil down. Breathe. Then the first question.
If it does not work: if anxiety is severe, ask the counselling service.

title: Saying no without over-explaining
source_document: ADDitude: The Lost Art of Saying No (Tuckman, 2026); Understood: ADHD and communicating boundaries (Aug 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. ADDitude article carries affiliate promotion and conflicting dates.
text:
Recognize it when: you say yes and then feel overwhelmed.
Technique: a short, kind refusal or a delay.
How: 1. Delay: Let me check my calendar and get back to you.
2. Short no: I am not available this weekend.
3. Capacity: I am at capacity this week. Ask me again next month.
4. Refer to someone else.
5. Save these phrases in your notes app.
Why it helps: A delay removes pressure to answer instantly, and short refusals avoid long justifications.
Try saying: Let me check and get back to you.
If it does not work: rehearse with a friend, starting with small requests.

title: You over-committed and dropped something
source_document: ADDitude: The Lost Art of Saying No (Tuckman, 2026); ADDitude: Hit Pause on ADHD Impulsivity (Barkley)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you forgot or cannot deliver what you promised.
Technique: admit it early and offer a fix.
How: 1. Say it: I forgot, I am sorry.
2. Offer a plan: Here is when I can do it, or who can.
3. Ask for more time early, not late.
4. Recall this when you are tempted to say yes next time.
Why it helps: Early honesty gives others time to find a backup and protects trust.
Try saying: I am sorry, I missed this. Here is my plan to fix it.
If it does not work: if it keeps happening, reduce commitments.

title: Overthinking a decision: 70% sure is enough
source_document: Understood podcast: Decisions, decisions (Feb 2026); URMC Behavioral Health Partners (Sep 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. The 70% rule is one guest's opinion.
text:
Recognize it when: you keep researching and cannot choose.
Technique: decide fast on reversible choices and slower on permanent ones.
How: 1. Separate the goal (why), the option (what) and the logistics (how).
2. Cut to two or three options.
3. Ask: Is this reversible? If yes, decide in minutes.
4. Aim for about 70% sure.
5. Ask someone not emotionally invested.
6. Remember not deciding is also a choice.
Why it helps: More options and treating reversible choices as permanent drive paralysis.
Try saying: If I am about 70% sure, that is enough.
If it does not work: set a timer of 5 to 15 minutes.

title: Which task first? Sticky notes and the urgent-important grid
source_document: Understood: Overthinking everything? Analysis paralysis (Jun 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: everything feels urgent and you cannot pick a first task.
Technique: put each task on a sticky note and sort.
How: 1. Write one task per note with a time estimate.
2. Sort into urgent/important and not.
3. Start with only the urgent and important group.
4. Say the next task out loud.
5. Take a short break if stuck, and ask if it is burnout.
Why it helps: Getting tasks out of your head lowers overwhelm.
Try saying: One note. One task. Start.
If it does not work: pick the smallest urgent task.

title: Name the fear behind the decision
source_document: ADDitude: Defeating Indecision (Maynard, 2011, updated 2021)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. Dated and anecdotal.
text:
Recognize it when: a decision feels huge and you cannot say why.
Technique: say the fear aloud and test it.
How: 1. Talk the options aloud.
2. Name the fear.
3. Ask: What is the worst realistic outcome and how would I cope?
4. Rank options by your values.
5. Pause to check you are not just being impulsive.
Why it helps: Fears feel huge in your head. Naming them shrinks them.
Try saying: What is the worst realistic outcome and could I cope?
If it does not work: talk it through with a friend.

title: Impulsive actions and purchases: pause and add friction
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Impulse Control Challenges (Apr 2026); ADDitude: Hit Pause on ADHD Impulsivity (Barkley)
source_citation: ADDA cites reviews and calls CBT promising, not proven. Barkley's advice is expert opinion.
text:
Recognize it when: you act or buy before thinking and regret it.
Technique: create a gap before acting and make the action harder.
How: 1. Count to five or take one slow breath.
2. Say: I need to check my schedule first.
3. Remove saved payment details and unsubscribe from sales.
4. Use a 24-hour rule for big decisions.
5. List your high-risk situations in advance.
Why it helps: A short gap breaks the automatic reaction, and friction reduces reliance on willpower.
Try saying: I will wait 24 hours.
If it does not work: protect sleep, since tired brains impulse more.

title: Blurting in conversation: reflect back and jot keywords
source_document: Psychology Today: Navigating Conversations with ADHD (Saline, May 2024); ADDitude: Are You Listening?
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique.
text:
Recognize it when: you jump in because you fear forgetting your point.
Technique: repeat back what you heard and jot a keyword.
How: 1. Write one keyword.
2. When they finish say: What I heard is __.
3. Then add your point.
4. Say: I have something to add but do not want to interrupt.
5. If you forget, follow up by text.
Why it helps: Notes remove the fear of forgetting, and reflecting shows you listened.
Try saying: I have something to add when you finish.
If it does not work: practise with a friend.

title: Verify you understood the instructions, then check each step
source_document: ADDitude: Are You Listening? (Novotni); ADDitude: ADHD at Work (Flippin, updated Apr 2026); CHADD: Remembering the Future (Dec 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no studies cited for the technique. CHADD's prospective memory piece cites mostly books and a children's review.
text:
Recognize it when: you start a task, then find you misunderstood or missed a step.
Technique: repeat the instructions back and use a check-off list for steps.
How: 1. Before starting say: Let me repeat that back.
2. Write the steps as a checklist.
3. Tick each as you finish.
4. Use an if-then cue: When I finish X, I check Y.
5. Add a 'did I actually do it?' check.
Why it helps: Repeating and ticking replaces fragile memory with a visible record.
Try saying: Let me repeat that back to be sure.
If it does not work: ask a colleague to verify the timing or the final step.
